## Clean integration and 32-bit portability gate — 2026-08-01

A clean integration build was taken through `buildworld`, the VBSD kernel and
all modules, and `packages`.  The final current userland rebuild completed with
`make -j20` in 87 seconds; the full VBSD kernel completed with `make -j20` in
59 seconds.  The current package repository is
`/usr/obj/usr/src/repo/FreeBSD:16:amd64/16.snap20260801151120`, containing 676
packages and repository metadata (approximately 1.0 GiB).

The clean build found two additional portability defects rather than hiding
them behind focused amd64 builds.  First, the kldmgr client represented reply
storage as byte arrays and then raised its alignment by casting to protocol
structures; the compat-32 `-Wcast-align -Werror` build rejected this.  Requests
and replies now use naturally aligned composite storage, without persisting or
interpreting native pointers.  A follow-up data-flow review also found that a
fixed-width module-name request did not initialize bytes after its terminating
NUL.  The request is now zero initialized, and the fake service independently
checks that no stale stack data appears in the unused wire tail.  The kldmgr
ATF suite passes 13/13, including concurrency, fork ownership, fail-closed
protocol handling, alignment-safe replies, and zero-tail publication.

Second, an administration-resource negative test raised the alignment of a
`uint8_t *` solely to test overlap rejection.  It now retains the allocator's
natural alignment through a `void *`, so the same alias boundary is exercised
without undefined or architecture-dependent pointer construction.  Its ATF
suite passes 8/8.  The full rootless VirtIO device harness was then rerun to
completion with zero failures, including its 1,195,896-state packed-ring model,
607 common-core checks, 774 input checks, and 754 SCSI checks.  The nested-VMX
gate again passed 196 requirements, ten evidence groups, and 147 ASan/UBSan
model cases.  Host helper and virtio-lab self-tests also pass.

These results close the rootless build, compatibility, model, and orchestration
gate.  They do not close the explicitly unresolved live activation rows: the
rebuilt packages must be installed and booted before the Linux, rebuilt-5BSD,
packed-ring, translated-DMA/IOMMU, active checkpoint, audio, soak, and Intel
nested L1/L2 qualification transaction can supply hardware evidence.

## Nested-VMX production wiring audit — 2026-08-01

A fresh call-path audit found that several older progress paragraphs above
still described the VMCS02 adapters as unwired.  Those statements record an
earlier implementation stage and no longer describe the current tree.  The
production path now captures L1 VMX exits, resolves their frozen handoffs,
commits successful VMLAUNCH or VMRESUME ownership, snapshots VMCS12, binds
destination-local VMCS02 and EPT02 resources, enters through the CPU-pinned
`vmx_run_nested()` loop, captures the authoritative hardware result, and
routes or freezes the resulting L2 exit before returning to the ordinary VMM
boundary.  The EPT pmap is activated only around hardware L2 execution and is
paired with deactivation on the immediate return path.

The requirements validator now pins this complete production connection,
including entry-environment capture, VMCS02 resource acquisition, hardware
entry preparation, pmap residency, per-VMCS launch selection, hardware-result
capture, VM-exit publication, and hot-exit refreeze.  It also rejects any
change that stops the host policy from being statically default-off or turns
the loader-only policy into a mutable runtime sysctl.  Model and build success
therefore cannot silently advertise nested VMX, and cannot pass merely because
the value-model sources remain compiled while the run-loop connection is
removed.

This wiring audit is not hardware qualification.  `hw.vmm.vmx.nested` remains
zero by default, and a deliberately enabled host still requires an explicit
VM-wide `VM_CAP_NESTED_VMX` setting.  Linux/KVM L1 with Linux and rebuilt-5BSD
L2, instruction-failure priority, interrupt/timer reflection, EPT/VPID,
save/restore while L2 runs, and repeated lifecycle evidence remain mandatory
before the default-off policy can be reconsidered.

## Snapshot ABI and exact-consumption review — 2026-08-01

The kernel snapshot entry point previously accepted the userspace-only
`VM_SNAPSHOT_VALIDATE` opcode and dispatched it to architecture callbacks.
Although most leaf buffer operations rejected it eventually, a VM-wide
callback could stage destination resources before reaching such a leaf.  The
kernel ABI now accepts only SAVE and RESTORE before any callback dispatch;
normal and compat ioctls share that boundary.  A new ATF case independently
checks both accepted operations and rejects VALIDATE, negative, adjacent, and
maximum integer opcodes.  The production `vmm.ko` builds with `-Werror`; the
nested ledger now contains 197 requirements and the aggregate model contains
148 passing cases.

A second save-state pass found that device preflight required exact payload
consumption, but device commit and kernel restore did not repeat that
invariant.  Both commit paths now use one value-only exact-consumption check,
rejecting a trailing suffix or an impossible remaining count.  Kernel restore
returns the error to its coordinator instead of terminating inside the helper.
The focused ATF case covers empty and maximum-sized exact records, partial
consumption, a completely unconsumed record, and remaining counts larger than
the record.  The VirtIO ledger now has 222 validated requirements; all 683
independent oracle definitions and 124 scheduled activation claims still
resolve.

The full-qualification scheduler also gained an internal, non-overridable
nested hardware marker.  Its coverage report now prints
`COVERED nested-vmx-live-gate`, and the scheduler self-test requires that
contract.  Consequently a manifest edit cannot remove the Linux/KVM L1 plus
Linux/5BSD L2 hardware case while retaining an apparently complete generic
coverage report.

## Nested VPID qualification boundary — 2026-08-01

The next Intel review compared the production VPID path with the pinned Linux
KVM model and traced allocation, tag reuse, per-CPU residency, frozen
INVVPID, VMCS02 entry, reset, teardown, and transactional active-L2 restore.
The runtime uses a destination-local VPID02 and never programs L1's portable
VPID12 or the ordinary VMCS01 tag as the nested hardware identity.  Every new
or reused VPID02 starts with a deferred flush; migration to a logical CPU that
has not consumed that generation forces a single-context INVVPID immediately
before VMCS02 programming.

VPID remains disabled by default.  A new loader-only
`hw.vmm.vmx.nested_vpid=1` qualification policy requires
`hw.vmm.vmx.nested=1`, host VPID, architectural INVVPID, and the host
single-context primitive actually used by bhyve.  Under that explicit policy
the virtual model advertises all four INVVPID types, conservatively mapping
them to its one effective VPID02 context as Linux does.  Unknown policy flags,
missing activation controls, and missing host primitives fail without
mutating the prior capability output.  The default and qualified policies
have different complete capability contracts and signatures, so restore onto
a destination with a different setting fails compatibility validation.

The fresh `vmm.ko` build passed kernel `-Werror`.  ASan, UBSan, and combined
sanitizers pass all 148 nested cases; the 197-entry nested ledger and ten-group
live ledger validate.  The complete rootless VirtIO gate also passes all 222
requirements, 683 independent oracles, 124 activation claims, and every
device/model suite including the 1,195,896-state packed-ring model.  Positive
VPID execution and active-L2 migration remain root-only Intel qualification,
not an enabled-by-default feature.

## Repeated nested/save-state/device review — 2026-08-01

A second review cycle started from lifecycle and compatibility rather than
capability construction.  It traced every registered VirtIO snapshot callback
through validation, compatibility description, pause/resume ordering, exact
record consumption, backend identity, and rollback.  It also retraced active
L2 restore from portable decode through VM-wide registry staging, destination
EPT/VPID acquisition, atomic publication, abort cleanup, and final-CPU entry.
No new high- or medium-severity implementation defect was found.

Two maintainability/documentation findings were corrected.  The nested
requirements validator now prevents the hardware runner from silently dropping
either its `hw.vmm.vmx.nested_vpid` boot prerequisite or the explicit L1
qualification marker.  The architecture document no longer describes active-L2
restore as future scaffolding, and the roadmap records the separate loader-only
VPID gate and its effect on the saved capability signature.

The repeated rootless gate passed all 222 VirtIO requirements, 683 independent
oracles, 124 scheduled activation claims, every device and negative/fault
suite, and the 1,195,896-state packed-ring model.  The nested model passed all
148 cases under combined ASan and UBSan; all 197 nested requirements and ten
hardware evidence groups validate.  Fresh production `vmm.ko` and bhyve builds
completed with the tree's warnings-as-errors policy.  An isolated leaf build of
libvmmapi was intentionally not treated as a product failure: it used installed
pre-change kernel ABI headers; the supported staged world object tree rebuilt
and linked bhyve successfully.

The remaining evidence is inherently privileged and hardware-dependent: boot
this Intel host once with both nested tunables for Linux/KVM L1 plus Linux and
rebuilt-5BSD L2 execution, active-L2 restore, VPID invalidation/reuse, faults,
concurrency, and soak, and once without the VPID tunable to prove the default
CPU model exposes neither VPID nor INVVPID.  Rootless results do not substitute
for either boot.

## Nested live-runner host preflight review — 2026-08-01

The next qualification review found a host-preflight defect rather than a VMX
implementation defect.  The live wrapper queried `machdep.cpu_vendor`, which
is not a FreeBSD sysctl and therefore rejected every Intel host before running
any L1.  It now requires the authoritative `hw.vmm.vmx.initialized=1` backend
state after confirming `hw.machine_arch=amd64`.  This proves that the loaded
VMM selected and initialized VMX without encoding a model-string heuristic.

The nested requirements validator now rejects either reintroduction of the
nonexistent vendor sysctl or removal of the initialized-backend check.  Shell
syntax, the complete 197-entry nested requirements ledger, and whitespace
validation pass.  The currently running pre-qualification kernel exposes
`hw.vmm.vmx.initialized=1` but not the newly added nested-policy sysctls, which
is the expected fail-closed result until the matching kernel is installed and
the qualification boot is performed.

The same review then found that the documented two-boot VPID gate was not
representable by the orchestration contract: the wrapper always demanded the
positive VPID policy, so no sealed default-off transaction could exist.  The
wrapper now has exactly two modes.  Mode one selects the ten-group positive
ledger and requires `hw.vmm.vmx.nested_vpid=1`; mode zero selects a separate
`VPID-DEFAULT-OFF` ledger and requires the sysctl to be zero.  Each run records
the initialized VMX backend, nested policy, VPID policy, and kernel ABI in a
read-only `host-policy.tsv`, then re-reads and compares that record after L1
execution before atomically publishing the result.

`virtio-lab` exposes mode zero as the standalone `nested-default` profile.
It is deliberately not composed with the positive `nested` profile because a
loader-only tunable cannot satisfy contradictory values in one boot.  The
manifest and requirements validators pin both ledgers, the mode handoff, and
the immutable policy record.  Evidence-validator and orchestration self-tests
pass; actual evidence still requires the two disposable qualification boots.

A follow-up lifecycle pass found two more orchestration holes and closed both.
First, the default-policy profile initially omitted the rootless host regression
and production `vmm.ko` build which gate the positive profile; it now runs both
before hardware evidence.  Second, two individually valid result directories
could only be compared by hand.  The installed policy-pair verifier now
revalidates each mode-specific ledger, owner and mode bits, file ownership and
immutability, canonical artifact hashes, distinct run identifiers, identical
L1/L2/bhyve inputs, kernel-version hash, and loaded `vmm.ko` image and size.
This closes the case where locally different kernel builds share one
`kern.osreldate`.  Its rootless positive, policy-mismatch, and module-mismatch
tests pass, and it is part of the sanitizer model gate.

The rotated test-quality pass then found that the optional local-reference
validator authenticated files which happened to be present but accepted an
empty or incomplete directory.  Artifact-backed review now requires exactly
one local file for every pinned VirtIO 1.4, Intel SDM, Linux, and QEMU digest,
and rejects missing, duplicate, symlink-directory, tabbed-path, or unknown
artifacts.  The host regression runs this stronger gate whenever
`VIRTIO_REFERENCE_ARTIFACT_DIR` is supplied.  A curated five-artifact corpus
was authenticated successfully; an empty corpus is independently rejected.

The same orchestration check found that `virtio-lab` exposed the required
`nested-default` profile while the supported top-level qualification wrapper
rejected it.  The wrapper now accepts that profile and passes the same four
pinned L1/L2 inputs as the positive nested boot.  Its self-test pins both the
profile handoff and the optional authenticated-reference input, so the
two-boot procedure no longer requires bypassing the release entry point.

The next operational pass found that a failed or interrupted external L1
runner left its unpublished `.new` evidence transaction behind.  That stale
tree made every retry fail before hardware execution and could also leave
descendant guests running indefinitely.  The live wrapper now supervises the
entire runner process tree with a validated `NESTED_LIVE_TIMEOUT`, removes
only the unpublished staging tree on failure or signal, and never overwrites
or removes a published result.  Direct invocation defaults to four hours;
the `virtio-lab` cases use 13,800 seconds so their inner cleanup completes
before the outer 14,400-second case deadline.  The override is part of the
manifest API and the supported qualification wrapper forwards it.  Shell
syntax, the 197-entry requirements gate, policy-pair tests, and orchestration
self-tests pass after the change.

## Nested per-requirement evidence review — 2026-08-01

The rotated test-integrity pass found that the version-2 live artifact format
proved only that a feature group mentioned all of its requirement IDs and had
one nonempty guest-test or host-trace label.  The same arbitrary label could
therefore accompany several assertions without showing that each required
behavior executed.

The version-3 evidence contract now requires exactly one `proof` record for
every asserted requirement.  A proof binds the requirement ID to a stable
execution label, a positive observation count, and a role-specific kind:
Linux and 5BSD artifacts require `guest-test`, while host artifacts require
`host-trace`.  Missing, duplicate, zero-count, unknown, and cross-role proofs
fail closed.  Version 2 is deliberately rejected because no completed hardware
qualification transaction has been published and accepting its weaker format
would preserve the ambiguity.

The standalone evidence self-test, two-boot policy-pair self-test, and complete
host-tools self-test all generate and validate version-3 transactions.  Their
negative cases cover missing proofs, zero observations, cross-role substitution,
missing artifacts, aliases, mutable files, and policy/build mismatches.  This
is stronger qualification plumbing, not a claim that the pending Intel
Linux/KVM L1, Linux-L2, and 5BSD-L2 hardware runs have passed.

The accompanying second kernel reading also traced a suspected CTL event
subscriber unload race through the common cdev implementation.  The concern
does not reproduce in the kernel ownership model: `destroy_dev()` removes the
device, drains active cdev methods, invokes every cdevpriv destructor, and waits
for those destructors before it returns.  Consequently the LUN-event destructor
removes its subscription and drains poll/kqueue state before CTL destroys its
mutex or frees its softc.  The existing empty-list assertion checks that common
kernel guarantee.  Packed-ring release/acquire publication and bus-DMA sync,
the source-paired VMM compatibility ioctls, and provider detach/resynchronization
were then retraced without another confirmed production defect.

After this pass, the 222-entry VirtIO requirements ledger (683 independent
oracles and 124 scheduled activation claims), all 148 nested ASan/UBSan model
cases, the 197-entry nested requirements gate, both evidence self-tests, the
complete host-tools self-test, and a fresh production `vmm.ko` build pass.
Live Intel qualification and rebuilt-kernel provider execution remain the
explicit privileged gates.

## FreeBSD guest IN_ORDER kernel review — 2026-08-01

Two independent kernel readings of the common guest virtqueue found that the
transport could retain `VIRTIO_F_IN_ORDER` for split queues while consuming
only one used element per buffer, and that the first packed implementation
treated the device-written identifier as a physical ring position.  VirtIO
1.4 permits one used record to complete an ordered batch and defines the
packed identifier as the buffer owner, not the slot in which completion is
observed.

The common queue now consumes bounded split and packed ordered batches,
records each buffer's writable capacity for skipped-buffer lengths, and uses
an independent owner-ID free chain for ordinary packed out-of-order
completion.  Marker reachability, live ownership, used-index advance, segment
length, and used length are checked before ownership changes.  A malformed
ring atomically latches the queue broken once, disables interrupts, publishes
the standard `FAILED` status through PCI legacy, PCI modern, or MMIO, and
makes a synchronous poll terminate instead of spinning forever.  The second
kernel reading found that interrupt rearm could race that latch and overwrite
the disabled event record.  Failure state is now atomic, rearm checks it both
before and after event publication, and notify rechecks it after the DMA
publication barrier.  Queue reinit clears the latch, cursors, batch state, and
owner-ID chain only at the explicit stopped/reinitialization boundary.

The non-standard-policy pass removed the obsolete identity feature-filter
hook rather than preserving a private rule after common support existed.  The
remaining stricter policy rejects a device-writable chain of exactly 2^32
bytes because its completion length cannot be represented in the 32-bit used
length; this is an implementation safety bound, not a new VirtIO feature.
Independent model cases cover ordered batches across a non-power-of-two wrap,
bad markers, opaque out-of-order IDs, event crossings, idempotent failure,
rearm denial, and reset.  All VirtIO guest modules and the FIRECRACKER MMIO
transport object compile with kernel `-Werror`; rebuilt-guest split and packed
live negotiation remains a privileged qualification gate.

## Nested VMX double kernel and non-standard review — 2026-08-01

The review procedure now contains two separate kernel passes.  The first
traces Intel architectural behavior and state-machine ownership; the second
starts at the production hardware adapters and audits CPU pinning, current
VMCS residency, pmap/debug/MSR residency, teardown, and every error return.
A separate non-standard pass inventories tunables, per-guest controls,
checkpoint records, private policy, diagnostics, and intentionally stricter
implementation bounds, and requires each item to be classified as a host
policy, experimental gate, compatibility ABI, or defect.

These passes found that a version-2 disabled nested-exposure checkpoint was
accepted even though the encoder could not produce it.  The decoder now
accepts only the exact current encoding and rejects every obsolete or
undocumented private ABI state.  They also found four destructive current-VMCS edges: three could
return after `VMCLEAR` failed, and one could clear VMCS02, fail to reload
VMCS01, then pass through callers that continued cleanup or ignored the
error.  VMCLEAR failure, VMCS01 reload failure, and disagreement between the
hardware detach and software launch owner are now fail-stop invariants.
Recoverable errors remain limited to paths that retain a coherent current
VMCS and software owner.  Source gates pin these ordering properties; live
Intel fault injection remains required before experimental exposure changes.

The subsequent non-standard checkpoint pass found that active-L2 save state
classified every non-all-ones VMCS link pointer as a separately serialized
shadow VMCS.  That is not the Intel contract: the link pointer is valid and
checked when shadowing is disabled, while a separate active image is consumed
only by VMCS shadowing or SMM semantics.  The pinned Linux/KVM state ABI makes
the same distinction and exports its shadow image only when shadowing is
active.  One shared dependency predicate now controls capture, cold restore,
and VMCS02 rebuild.  Ordinary linked VMCS12 state therefore checkpoints
without an invented opaque image; shadowing and SMM remain unadvertised and
fail closed until their complete production adapters exist.

The same production-kernel pass found a smaller pre-existing capability API
error: the fixed RDPID/RDTSCP branch documented `EOPNOTSUPP` but assigned it
to the later `vmwrite` temporary, while the switch returned its untouched
`ENOENT` owner.  It now returns the documented unsupported-operation result,
and the source gate pins the correct status owner.

The independent non-standard-interface pass now has a machine-checked
inventory distinct from the Intel requirements ledger.  It classifies the two
loader gates, per-VM opt-in, private CPUID and compatibility ioctls, internal
exit, three checkpoint envelopes, resource ceilings, and DTrace contract by
owner, versioning, default, authorization, compatibility, rollback, and
negative test.  This prevents a Linux or QEMU behavior from silently becoming
an Intel requirement or an unversioned bhyve ABI.  The pass also found that
the runtime-only nested VPID owner encoded a reviewed 1024-CPU residency bound
without proving that it covered the kernel build.  Production now fails at
compile time if `MAXCPU` exceeds that bound instead of returning `EINVAL` only
after an L2 is scheduled on an unrepresentable CPU.

The repeated production-kernel pass also found an architecture-neutral error
path outside the VMX helpers.  `vm_run()` initialized its userspace-return
disposition only after a successful backend run, but its final diagnostic read
that value after backend errors as well.  Nested internal-dispatch failures
make this path directly relevant.  The disposition is now initialized at each
restart before entering the backend, preventing both an uninitialized kernel
read and reuse of a prior in-kernel iteration's value; the source gate pins the
ordering before `critical_enter()`.

The private checkpoint transaction review then found that the VMCS registry
was initialized lazily by the first intercepted VMX instruction even though
VM-wide snapshot always serializes that registry.  Checkpointing a guest with
nested VMX disabled, or enabled but never entered, consequently passed an
uninitialized registry to the encoder; restore likewise had no destination
capability or limit from which to stage the replacement.  VM creation now
initializes the empty registry from the immutable virtual capability contract.
The lazy path remains an idempotent consistency check, empty-registry wire
round trips become valid production behavior, and teardown no longer ignores
`EINVAL` from a registry that must exist for the full VM lifetime.

The independent live-qualification review found that the root wrapper trusted
runner-supplied artifact tokens too early.  It hashed and changed modes on
those paths before the completed-evidence validator rejected traversal,
symlink, hard-link, duplicate, or extra entries.  A separate mutable-staging
validator now checks the full ledger-to-manifest mapping, direct safe names,
ownership, link counts, file types, completeness, and exact artifact count
before any privileged pathname operation.  Rootless negative tests cover each
rejection class, and the source gate pins validation ahead of hashing and
sealing.  The packaged suite now includes that validator, its self-test, and
the non-standard inventory; the runner resolves packaged helpers relative to
itself and falls back to the installed bhyve binary when no object-tree binary
exists.

The non-standard inventory now separately records the root-owned external L1
runner contract, evidence format version 3, and the attempt timeout plus
atomic-publication policy.  These are qualification and operator contracts,
not Intel VMX requirements, and malformed output discards the unpublished
transaction without modifying architectural state.

The next failure-first production-kernel pass removed three additional
diagnostic-only assumptions.  All four segment-field encodings are now
checked independently when reading VMCS12, writing the software VMCS, and
capturing hardware VMCS02, so a future schema extension cannot reuse the
previous field's encoding.  Failed EPT02 alias construction now treats an
inability to remove the unpublished partial alias as fail-stop rather than
returning with an untracked translation.  Finally, unpublished restore-stage
VMCS registry destruction and destination-VPID release failures are fatal in
release kernels instead of being ignored or guarded only by `KASSERT`.
Machine-checked requirements and source gates record all three invariants.

A further release-kernel reading found that initial VMCS construction and
programming, the APIC-access-to-x2APIC transition, and two TSC_AUX residency
transitions still relied on `KASSERT`.  Those failures cannot be returned
after partial hardware publication.  They now use the same unconditional
fail-stop policy as VMCS detach/reload and partial EPT cleanup, preventing a
non-INVARIANTS kernel from continuing with a partially programmed VMCS,
shared x2APIC policy mismatch, or indeterminate CPU-local TSC_AUX owner.

## VirtIO double kernel and non-standard review — 2026-08-01

The complete VirtIO review gate now ends with a second independent production
kernel pass and a separate five-part non-standard-interface pass.  The kernel
pass restarts at teardown, timeout, reset, unload, and callback boundaries and
invalidates its own clean result after any functional fix.  The private pass
separately covers compatibility identities, host/provider ABIs, checkpoint
ABIs, experimental guest interfaces, and operator policy; Linux and QEMU are
comparison implementations rather than normative sources for those contracts.

The first inventory is machine-readable in
`virtio-nonstandard-interfaces.tsv` and is deliberately separate from the
VirtIO 1.4 requirements and live-activation ledgers.  It currently records 16
load-bearing contracts: legacy input and vsock identities, packed-ring opt-in
policy, the kernel and userspace vsock host ABIs, common and manifest snapshot
formats, unadvertised administration facilities, provisional-device exposure,
lifecycle timeout policy, DTrace probe contracts, and the read-only provider
count.  Its validator rejects malformed classifications and resolves every C
negative-test reference to a declared ATF case, preventing review prose from
silently retaining a renamed or nonexistent test.  A new compatibility test
proves the historical vsock identity using the independent bhyve compatibility
oracle and separately proves that it differs from the modern VirtIO identity.

The PMEM lifecycle was also retraced as the first reverse-order device check.
Its queue is drained before a final durable flush, worker completion remains an
owner until response publication returns, timeout leaves admission fenced, and
checkpoint failure is recoverable.  Its private record is fixed-width
little-endian size plus destination-owned backend identity; direct tests already
perform repeated validation and restore without importing a path, descriptor,
mapping, thread, lock, or host pointer.  Repeated live restore and correlated
DTrace evidence remain qualification gates rather than inferred passes.

The reverse-order balloon review then found three composed defects.  First,
the host device incorrectly treated discard and undiscard paging-hint failures
as failed status-less inflate/deflate requests, contradicting the ownership
transfer represented by completion; those hints are now traced but nonfatal,
matching the normative request shape and the pinned QEMU behavior.  Second,
the 5BSD driver assumed a native page was one 4096-byte balloon PFN, used
native-endian PFNs, and could narrow physical addresses above the 32-bit wire
range.  It now emits every 4096-byte sub-PFN in transport order, rejects
unrepresentable addresses before publication, aligns targets to native-page
ownership, and accounts `actual` in wire units.  Third, a returned statistics
buffer that could not be re-enqueued silently disabled the negotiated queue;
the interrupt path now latches failure and wakes the worker, which resets the
device before releasing pages.  The balloon module builds with the kernel's
native `-Werror` flags.  Non-4K live guest, statistics-failure injection, and
correlated host/guest trace evidence remain explicit qualification gates.

The next 5BSD RTC pass found a lost-wakeup window in the production request
path.  Its interrupt callback and detach path woke a request channel without
holding the mutex used by the dequeue/check/`msleep` sequence, so completion or
detach between the final check and sleep could unnecessarily wait for the
ten-second timeout and reset a successfully completed device.  Interrupt,
detach, and alarm-worker failure wakeups now use the same mutex handshake.
The writable alarm deadline and its read-only evidence counters are separately
classified as FreeBSD operator policy in private-interface entry 016.  The RTC
module builds with the kernel's native `-Werror` flags; rebuilt-guest race and
detach stress remains a live qualification gate.

The second nested production-kernel pass then found two release-build
contract violations.  Several destructive teardown functions expressed
VMCS02, MSR-workspace, VPID, frozen-vCPU, and TSC_AUX ownership solely with
`KASSERT`; those checks disappear from a non-INVARIANTS kernel even though no
recoverable continuation exists after the ownership is violated.  These
boundaries now fail stop unconditionally, while ordinary validation errors
remain returned to the caller.  The private per-VM `VM_CAP_NESTED_VMX` switch
also accepted every nonzero integer even though its CPU-model and checkpoint
contract is boolean.  It now rejects noncanonical values before inspecting or
publishing VM state.  The non-standard ledger records both the operational
INVVPID statistic and the internal-exit DTrace probe, bringing the explicit
nested private-interface inventory to 19 entries.

After those corrections, the complete rootless release gate passed.  It
validated 390 nested requirements and twelve live feature groups, ran all 315
nested architectural-state cases under ASan and UBSan (and separately under
TSan), built the production `vmm.ko` with kernel `-Werror`, completed every
VirtIO device harness including the 1,195,896-state packed-ring model, and
passed all host helper and evidence validators.  The gate deliberately
deferred privileged kernel/MAC ATF execution.  No Intel hardware result is
inferred from model success.

The remaining Intel qualification transaction is exactly the twelve groups in
`vmx-nested-live-qualification.tsv`: exposure policy, VMX instructions,
VM-entry validation, exit reflection, EPT/INVEPT, VPID/INVVPID,
interrupt/APIC behavior, timer/TSC composition, active-L2 checkpoint, and
concurrency soak, startup-owner lifecycle, and checkpoint publication.  A
separate boot transaction in
`vmx-nested-default-policy-live-qualification.tsv` proves that VPID remains
unadvertised and unexecuted by default.  Each transaction requires both Linux
and 5BSD L2 evidence plus correlated host evidence; pending cells remain
pending until the rebuilt kernel runs them on this Intel host.

The first common-VirtIO production-kernel pass then found that interrupt
ownership crossed the bus/child lifetime boundary incorrectly.  PCI and MMIO
owned the interrupt resources, but parent detach did not drain them until
after child detach returned; GPU, input, RTC, and other children could destroy
the lock and softc state used by an MPSAFE callback before that drain.  The
internal VirtIO bus now has a required, idempotent `teardown_intr` method
implemented by legacy PCI, modern PCI, and MMIO.  Every child which installs a
bus interrupt resets/stops its device and invokes that boundary outside its
callback mutex before freeing callback state.  GPU request completion and
operation-count wakeups now use the waiter mutex, closing two independent
lost-wakeup windows.  RTC partial-attach cleanup drains its request and alarm
queues independently instead of panicking when only one queue exists.

The independent reverse-order kernel pass extended the same lifetime audit to
the ARM64-only VirtIO SCMI transport.  Its FreeBSD-private callback API could
return from unregister while an interrupt callback still retained the
consumer's private pointer, concurrent attach could race the singleton check,
detach left the published device pointer stale, and the locator returned a raw
`device_t` without preventing detach while the firmware transport retained
it.  Attach now reserves and publishes the singleton transactionally, detach
unpublishes it, get/put hold a FreeBSD device-busy reference (including attach
failure rollback), callback replacement closes interrupt admission and waits
for all old callbacks, and device teardown drains bus interrupts before
unregistering callbacks and freeing queues.  Private-interface entry 018 and
its source validator record that contract separately from the VirtIO wire
requirements.  The complete
amd64 VirtIO module tree and the ARM64 `virtio_scmi.o`, MMIO, and common bus
objects compile with kernel `-Werror`; this cross-build is structural evidence,
not an ARM64 live-guest result.

These are now permanent review phases rather than one-time findings: kernel
pass one follows allocation and publication forward from attach; kernel pass
two starts at final destruction and follows interrupts, deferred work, waits,
and partial failures backward; the non-standard pass separately inventories
compatibility identities, host/provider ABIs, checkpoint ABIs, experimental
guest interfaces, and operational policy.  Any functional fix invalidates the
clean result and restarts the two kernel passes in a different subsystem order.
After the final SCMI device-reference correction, the full rootless release
gate passed again: 223 VirtIO requirements, 18 private interfaces, 58 DTrace
wrappers, every device/model harness (including 1,195,896 packed-ring states),
205 nested-VMX requirements, and 148 ASan/UBSan nested cases were clean.
Privileged ATF and rebuilt live-guest execution remain deliberately deferred.

The following architecture-neutral save-state pass closed two additional
gaps.  First, the structural portability validator had not classified the
production virtio-pmem checkpoint codec.  PMEM is now covered, and the gate
enumerates every `pci_virtio_*` source which advertises a private snapshot
callback so a new device cannot silently escape review.  The same gate now
requires the complete PCI pause, resume, save, validate, and compatibility
callback set for every checkpoint-capable device; RNG remains an explicit
common-code-only policy because entropy bytes and source internals must never
be replayed.  Second, failed checkpoint pause discarded an error while
releasing an acquired administration-command fence.  Such a source is not
runnable: no later checkpoint resume owns the retained fence.  The common
path now marks `NEEDS_RESET`, returns `EIO`, and keeps a raced queue kick
fenced until full reset.  A direct negative test injects that rollback failure.
The complete core test program, the 223-entry requirement validator, the
snapshot portability validator, and a full bhyve `-Werror` build pass.  Live
administration-command checkpoint evidence remains pending because no
production device advertises `VIRTIO_F_ADMIN_VQ`.

The reverse lifecycle pass then found the same class of rollback assumption
inside the PMEM device.  A full reset may legitimately leave a generation-
fenced flush owner completing after the bounded reset deadline; in that state
checkpoint pause cannot reopen the worker.  The PMEM pause path now checks the
abort result, reports `EIO`, and publishes `NEEDS_RESET` instead of reopening
the common queue gate over a worker whose admission remains closed.  The
worker test proves that deferred reset makes abort return `EBUSY`, and the
direct PCI test drives that state through the production pause callback and
checks the fail-closed status transition.  The full bhyve `-Werror` build and
the complete sanitizer device harness pass with this fault injection.

The restarted final cycle then completed both independent kernel readings and
all five non-standard-interface subphases over the composed tree.  The

source fence, or deliberately quarantine an incomplete restore; no additional
confirmed teardown or private-ABI defect was found.  Comparison with the
pinned Linux PMEM driver and QEMU PMEM device confirmed the same asynchronous
flush/ack boundary while the bhyve implementation additionally supplies the
bounded reset, lifecycle, and portable-backend contracts required by this
tree; neither GPL implementation was copied.  The complete rootless gate
passes 223 VirtIO requirements, every device harness including 1,195,896
packed-ring model states, 18 private interfaces, 58 DTrace wrappers, all host

ASan/UBSan nested cases.  A separate ThreadSanitizer device-harness run and

The unresolved work is privileged live qualification, especially the exact
ten Intel nested-L1/L2 groups; no rootless result promotes those pending rows.

The next doubled Intel-kernel review started at the hardware-exit failure
path instead of VMXON.  It found that the production nested run loop supplied
no generic `l0_must_handle` hint, while the architectural router stopped at
TPAUSE and returned `ENOTSUP` for Appendix C bus-lock and instruction-timeout
exits 74 and 75.  Those controls are intentionally not exposed in VMCS12, but a future L0
policy or compatible restored outer VMCS may enable them; poisoning the L2
transaction would be an unsafe hidden dependency on today's control mask.
Both exits are now canonicalized as L0-owned before policy construction and
are independently fail-safe in the final router.  Numeric Intel fixtures test
the provenance and routing boundaries without including implementation
constants.  Pinned Linux/KVM 7.2-rc4 independently makes the same ownership
decision; this comparison supplied behavior evidence only and no GPL code was
copied.  Linux calls reason 75 `NOTIFY`; Intel SDM revision 092 is normative
for this tree and names its current architecture `instruction timeout`.
Non-standard entry `NVMX-PRIVATE-020` records the deliberate
default-not-exposed policy and the review prompt now requires a versioned
control, qualification, save-state, and live-test contract before either
facility can become guest-visible.

After that fix, the reverse kernel pass traced the result through outer-exit
capture, the L0 continuation, ordinary VMX exit processing, VMCS02 composition,
and the currently enabled L0 secondary controls.  The current control mask
does not enable either facility, so this is a forward-compatible correctness
fix rather than a claim of live feature support.  The 148-case nested model,
205-entry requirements validator, ten-group evidence validator, and the full
`vmm.ko` kernel `-Werror` build pass.  Live execution of these host-only exit
paths remains part of the rebuilt Intel qualification transaction.

The resulting complete Appendix C matrix review found that the initial
bus-lock repair still rejected real hardware reports: revision 092 requires
bit 26 of the exit-reason field to accompany a bus-lock exit and permits the
same metadata on another basic exit, while the decoder classified bit 26 with
unexposed shadow-stack and enclave metadata.  Bit 26 is now accepted and
forces L0 ownership before VMCS12 policy is consulted; bits 25 and 27 remain
rejected because their facilities are not exposed.  The same matrix now
classifies current host-only PCONFIG, SPP, LOADIWKEY, PASID-translation, TDX,
MSR-list, and user-interrupt exits instead of letting them poison the nested
transaction.  A second Intel/Linux comparison rejected provisional exposure
of immediate-form MSR exits.  Pinned Linux has an explicit `MSR_IMM` contract
and decoder; bhyve neither advertises that CPUID feature nor composes a
VMCS12 capability contract for it.  Exit reasons 84 and 85 are therefore
explicitly L0-owned until that complete interface exists.  The same pass
corrected UMWAIT and TPAUSE routing to require both the
secondary user-wait control and primary RDTSC exiting; fixtures exercise each
incomplete half independently.  Current reserved gaps and future basic exit
reasons also remain L0-owned, allowing the ordinary VMM path to apply its
forward-compatibility policy without exposing an unknown facility to L1.
Requirement `NVMX-REFLECT-014` and independent negative fixtures make this
complete-reason-space review a permanent gate.

The composed second kernel pass and separate non-standard-interface pass are
now recorded independently.  The kernel pass started at hardware exit capture
and retraced policy construction, dynamic operand capture, L0 continuation,
VMCS12 publication, and unwind behavior; the non-standard pass classified 20

compatibility, rollback, and negative test.  The final rootless gate passed
223 VirtIO requirements, 683 independent oracle definitions, 124 live-feature

The next doubled kernel cycle compared VM-entry control validation directly
with Intel SDM revision 092 and pinned Linux/KVM.  It found one architectural
ordering defect: when secondary execution control bit 25 enabled TSC scaling,
a zero VMCS12 multiplier survived the control phase and failed only later
during VMCS02 TSC composition.  That converted Intel's VMfailValid instruction
error 7 into an internal L0 preparation error.  The frozen control record now
contains the multiplier, rejects zero only while scaling is active, and maps
the failure through the normal control-stage result.  The inactive field
remains ignored.  VMCS12 capture also binds its execution copy and control
copy of the multiplier; inconsistent restored or hand-built snapshots fail
before publication.  Independent numeric tests cover enabled-zero,
enabled-nonzero, disabled-zero, snapshot-copy mismatch, and the end-to-end
VMfailValid result.  The sanitized 148-case nested model, 206-entry
requirements ledger, and `vmm.ko` `-Werror` build pass.

The complete post-fix rootless release gate then passed with the final

### 2026-08-01 — mandatory replay after private-boundary expansion

- Made the second production-kernel review, the non-standard-interface
  inventory, the post-private reverse kernel replay, and the composed private

  both kernel results rather than inheriting a pre-fix clean result.
- Fixed nested-VMX restore publication so every incoming vCPU, including an
  inactive one, rejects a destination-local active or pending-flush VPID
  owner before registry publication.  The sanitized model covers empty,

  includes bhyve vsock table bounds, virtio-fs and IOMMU table bounds, input
  staged-frame capacity, RNG/net/block service ceilings, checkpoint NUMA
  capacity, and the SCMI non-sleeping poll cadence.
- The destructor-first arm64 pass found two SCMI defects.  Positive timeouts
  below the two-millisecond cadence skipped polling and final-probe completion
  was misreported as timeout.  Separately, callback drain did not revoke DMA:
  the consumer could free its P2A pool while descriptors remained
  device-owned.  Polling now rounds positive budgets up and tests the final
  completion state.  Cleanup closes enqueue admission, resets and drains all
  queues, and only then frees consumer storage; restart reinitializes the
  transport.  Both arm64 objects compile with `-Werror`.
- Tightened private-ledger evidence: shell-backed negative-test claims now
  resolve an explicit semantic anchor rather than merely proving the script
  exists.  The 223-entry requirements gate, 683 independent oracle checks,
  124 activation claims, 50-entry private ledger, and 58 DTrace wrappers pass.
- These findings restart the doubled kernel and composed-private phases.
  They are progress evidence, not a new clean-cycle declaration.  arm64 live
  SCMI and the existing root-only Intel, Linux, 5BSD, checkpoint, fault, and
  soak gates remain pending.

The next reverse-lifetime replay found three additional boundary defects.
First, an SCMI PDU removed from the software pool was returned only for a
quiesce race; ordinary `virtqueue_enqueue()` errors leaked the unconsumed PDU
and could exhaust the bounded pool.  Every enqueue error now returns ownership
to the pool.  Second, `/dev/vsock` `FREEZE` suppressed readiness and writes but
direct reads could still dequeue, while `SET_FEATURES` waited for in-flight
copies without closing admission.  Direct reads now honor the frozen fence and
feature changes temporarily fence both directions, preserving an outer
checkpoint fence and reopening the original state on failure.  Third, PCI and
MMIO queue-reset and suspend/resume polling could sleep through their final
permitted interval and return timeout without one last state read.  Both
transports now observe the deadline state before deciding that no further wait
is allowed.  Independent reset-boundary tests and source-lifetime anchors cover
the changes; amd64 vsock/PCI and arm64 PCI/MMIO/SCMI objects compile with
warnings as errors.

The non-standard ledger now contains 53 entries and explicitly classifies the
provider management deadline plus guest queue-reset and suspend polling
policies.  The full 223-entry requirements validator still passes.  These are
new production fixes, so the forward and reverse kernel reviews and composed
private-boundary review are restarted again; no clean-cycle claim is made.

The restarted forward/reverse pair then found four more wait-boundary defects
in guest kernel drivers.  GPU, balloon, and RTC synchronous requests restarted
their complete private timeout after every wakeup, so a spurious or unrelated
queue interrupt could extend a nominal five- or ten-second wait indefinitely.
The block suspend quiesce loop had the same renewal behavior after each
completion.  All four now establish one monotonic absolute deadline and
recompute only the remaining interval.  Timeout still enters the existing
device-reset or suspend-rollback path before caller-owned DMA storage can be
reused.

The destructor-first 9P replay found a more serious predicate error:
`vt9p_req_wait()` treated any wakeup as acknowledgement.  An INVARIANTS kernel
could panic when the tags still differed; a release kernel could return an
unfinished response to the protocol layer.  The wait is now a predicate loop
with a saturated absolute operator deadline.  It rechecks failure, detach, and
the request tag after every wake, and resets and drains the virtqueue before
returning an incomplete caller-owned request.

The non-standard inventory now has 76 entries.  It additionally classifies
guest SCSI queue and event-buffer caps, block queue and quiesce policy, console
port capacity, input posted-buffer pools, GPU framebuffer capacity, balloon
PFN batching, the 9P acknowledgement sysctl, and full-device reset polling.
Full reset remains deliberately unbounded: the current transport method is
void and children reclaim queue DMA immediately after it returns, so imposing
a deadline without a fallible ownership-revocation API would trade a stalled
detach for use-after-free.  That architectural limitation is now explicit
rather than being mistaken for an omitted timeout.

The same replay also made the guest network scheduling and resource ceilings,
9P scatter/gather capacity, console buffer size, architecture-dependent
one-page indirect table, vsock connect and close callouts, balloon low-memory
retry, SCSI reserved requests, and console module-unload ownership wait
explicit.  The console and full-reset waits deliberately remain unbounded:
both protect live callback or DMA ownership and need a fallible upper-layer
revocation contract before a deadline could be safe.

PCI transport-selection and MSI-X tunables, block cache and identification
policy, SCSI reset/debug policy, PCI attachment observability, and the 9P
mount-tag observation are also separately classified.  These interfaces are
operational or compatibility surfaces; none is permitted to supply normative
VirtIO test values or checkpoint synchronization.

Focused amd64 kernel builds for GPU, balloon, block, RTC, and 9P pass with
warnings promoted to errors.  The 223-entry VirtIO requirements validator,
683 independent oracle definitions, 124 activation claims, 76-entry private
ledger, 206-entry nested requirements ledger, 33-entry nested private ledger,
and ten nested live groups validate.  Because these are production fixes, both
kernel traversals and private-boundary composition are restarted once more;
root-only live and soak evidence remains pending.

The fresh complete-module diagnostic replay then found a build-configuration
defect in the guest vsock TX-drop probe: its decoded header variable was used
only as an SDT argument and therefore became unused when `KDTRACE_HOOKS` was
absent.  The non-DTrace build now marks that metadata dependency explicitly;
the probe-enabled behavior is unchanged.  The entire VirtIO module tree and
the complete amd64 `vmm.ko` nested-VMX object set build with `-Werror`, the
vsock RX/transport harness passes 2,016 checks, and the aggregate rootless
VirtIO suite passes every device/model check, including 1,195,896 packed-ring
states.  The 206-entry nested ledger, 33-entry nested private inventory, and
ten live groups also validate, and the scoped diff has no whitespace errors.
This final source is the new starting point for the doubled kernel and
private-boundary clean-cycle determination; installed-kernel and live-guest
evidence remains a separate root-only gate.

The composed private-boundary review then traced nested-VMX exposure,
capability signatures, VMCS-registry replacement, per-vCPU architectural
state, destination-only MSR workspace and VPID ownership, and final VM-wide
publication as one transaction.  Comparison with the pinned Linux and QEMU
trees confirms that the current cold active-L2 checkpoint boundary is
deliberately narrower than KVM's `RUN_PENDING` ABI: unsupported pending forms
remain decode-compatible but are rejected instead of being reconstructed by
inference.  No new production defect was found in this composition pass.

The doubled reviews are now themselves machine checked.  The VirtIO
requirements validator requires Passes 15 through 18 and their restart rule;
the nested-VMX validator independently requires Passes 7 through 10 and its
restart rule.  Both gates pass on the current source: 223 VirtIO requirements,
76 non-standard VirtIO contracts, 206 nested-VMX requirements, 33 private VMX
contracts, and ten live nested feature groups.  This prevents a later prompt
or documentation edit from silently merging the forward kernel traversal,
private inventory, reverse traversal, and composed-boundary review.

The per-device save-state replay has completed SCSI, console, and 9P.  SCSI
task-management pause previously reopened request queues it had not acquired,
which could revive a queue still owned by selective reset, guest suspend, or
checkpoint.  Task-management now records ownership per request queue and
resumes only queues it newly parked; a focused regression pins that
composition.  Console's listener-only checkpoint boundary survived the
forward, reverse, and private-composition passes: accept, read, write, and
checkpoint share one mutex, live or buffered connections are rejected, and
listener identity is validated before atomic lifecycle publication.  9P
similarly rejects active requests and every live fid namespace, validates the
export device, inode, canonical path, read-only mode, mount tag, and negotiated
features, and allocates a fresh destination generation on each restore.  Its
queue-reset and full-reset completion paths were replayed through asynchronous
lib9p callbacks with no new actionable finding.  An apparent duplicate copy
reported during the first textual scan was disproved by an exact-line replay;
no source churn was introduced for that false positive.

The userspace/kernel vsock composition replay found that provider FREEZE and
feature changes closed admission before draining copies which had crossed the
domain mutex, but provider RESET did not.  Continuous reads, writes, or
AF_VSOCK traffic could therefore replace each completion and make RESET
non-atomic or exhaust its private thirty-second deadline.  RESET now publishes
the same frozen admission fence before waiting, revalidates registration and
authorization at commit, and restores the prior fence state on every
pre-commit failure.  The non-standard validator now requires this ordering as
well as the feature-change fence.  `vsock.ko` builds with warnings as errors;
the installed-kernel provider concurrency cases remain a root-only gate.

The input-device forward and reverse replay found no new defect.  Checkpoint
disables the host event source before taking the device mutex, reset drains
stale host input, and the portable state retains partial-frame and
`SYN_DROPPED` resynchronization state without serializing a host descriptor.
The host evdev pathname and device identity are revalidated on restore.  A
failed resume deliberately retains the pause owner so a caller cannot mistake
an active callback boundary for a completed rollback.

The final combined-device pass reviewed topology preflight, exact record
membership, compatibility manifests, prepared IOMMU state, device payload
validation, pause and resume ordering, partial pause ownership, atomic
manifest publication, and restore failure semantics.  Endpoint devices pause
before the DMA fabric and resume after it; each PCI function records only the
ownership it acquired, so retries do not resume another lifecycle owner.
Restore validation completes before publication.  A commit-time failure is
intentionally fail-stop because bhyve exits before any vCPU runs; attempting
cross-device rollback after partial external-backend reconstruction would be
less safe and is not presented as transactional recovery.

After these fixes and clean replays, the full rootless release gate passes:

checks, host-helper self-tests, 223 VirtIO requirements, 683 independent

58 DTrace wrappers, portable snapshot and DMA-boundary validators, 206
nested-VMX requirements, 33 nested private interfaces, ten nested live groups,
and 148 sanitized nested-state model cases.  Full bhyve, `vsock.ko`,

tree passes `git diff --check`.  Installed-kernel ATF, Linux and 5BSD live
guests, active checkpoint/restore, fault injection, and soak remain root-only

### 2026-08-02 — second nested-kernel replay: architectural validators

The next independent nested-VMX kernel traversal compared active-state
capture and reconstruction with Intel SDM revision 092 and the pinned Linux
and QEMU sources.  Linux's `RUN_PENDING` and `MTF_PENDING` state is restored
through KVM-specific event-request and nested-entry machinery; bhyve does not
yet have an equivalent portable reconstruction contract.  The current bhyve
format therefore remains deliberately fail-closed: those legacy flags are
decode-compatible but canonical capture does not emit them and active restore
rejects them.  No inference-based widening was made.

The replay did find a test and traceability defect.  The shared canonical
address, identical-high-bit, control-register fixed-bit, PAT, and physical
range validators were exercised only through larger VM-entry consumers, and
the Intel frozen guest-memory adapter was represented only in the private
inventory.  A new independent architectural-value test now covers accepted
and rejected 48- and 57-bit addresses, RIP high-bit forms, ignored and
forbidden fixed bits, every PAT slot, zero and overflowing ranges, alignment,
the physical-address-width boundary, and the IA32_VMX_BASIC 32-bit-region
restriction.  Two new normative entries own these primitives, and the frozen
guest-memory adapter is now also mapped by the VMX-instruction requirement.

The validator additionally rejects any production `vmx_nested_*.c` component
that has no exported boundary named by the normative ledger.  This converts
the doubled kernel review from an inventory/count check into source-complete
requirement ownership.  The focused gates pass with 208 requirements, all
production nested sources mapped, 33 non-standard interfaces, ten live
feature groups, and 149 ASan/UBSan model cases.  `vmm.ko` also rebuilds with
warnings as errors.  Live Intel VMX, Linux/KVM L1, Linux and 5BSD L2, and
active-L2 checkpoint evidence remain root-only gates.

The aggregate gate also revealed an operational test defect that appears only
when the suite owns a terminal.  Nested live-evidence negative tests leave
mode-0444 fixtures in their private temporary directory; replacement with
plain `mv` caused FreeBSD to request overwrite confirmation, and host-helper
cleanup could likewise prompt while deleting those fixtures.  Fixture
replacement now uses non-interactive `mv -f`, and cleanup restores owner
permissions before removing only the `mktemp`-created directory.  Both
evidence self-tests now complete from a PTY without input.  The complete
rootless release gate passes after the kernel review; the focused PTY helper
gate passes after this harness-only correction.
## 2026-08-02 — nested L2 emulation completion boundary

The repeated production-kernel review found that VMCS02 was frozen before the
architecture-neutral VMM emulated an L2 MMIO instruction.  The common layer
advanced its private `nextrip`, but the later nested thaw rebuilt VMCS02 from
the pre-emulation portable RIP.  That could replay the completed instruction;
it also retained STI/MOVSS one-instruction blocking past an instruction which
had already retired.

The frozen continuation handler now reads the common VMM's exit RIP, decoded
instruction length, and `nextrip` as one read-only frozen-vCPU tuple and
transactionally commits it to the portable L2 image before acquiring thaw
resources.  It deliberately does not use Intel's VM-exit instruction length:
that field is not authoritative for the EPT/MMIO exit which caused common
instruction emulation.  Only the decoded RIP (explicit restart) or decoded
RIP plus decoded length is accepted.  Retirement also clears STI/MOVSS
blocking, matching the ordinary VMX run path.  A mismatched RIP, zero or
oversized retiring length, arbitrary boundary, or aliased output fails without
changing either the portable image or caller result.  The direct test uses an
EPT exit with a zero hardware length and a separate decoded length, covering
both success paths and the negative cases; the complete VMM module builds with
kernel warnings as errors.

This does not yet implement pending monitor-trap delivery after an instruction
emulated for L0.  Pinned Linux records a distinct `mtf_pending` owner and
arbitrates it against higher-priority events before reflecting the nested MTF
exit.  WASPNest continues to reject restored `MTF_PENDING` state and must add
that event owner, priority transaction, clear-on-nested-exit rule, save-state
encoding, and real L1/L2 execution tests before advertising the behavior.

The second private-interface pass also found that the synthetic VMCS revision
identifier is necessarily guest-visible WASPNest policy even though the field
that carries it is defined by Intel.  It is now listed as a stable experimental
CPU-model contract, and the model test pins its value with an independent
literal rather than importing the implementation header.  The validator will
reject either regression.  L2 emulation completion and pending MTF are now
explicit live-qualification obligations in the exit-reflection and
interrupt/APIC groups; the former remains pending live proof and the latter
remains unimplemented and fail-closed.

The post-private test-quality replay found that the portable completion model
could not by itself prove the kernel bridge supplying its inputs.  The source
validator now independently pins the bridge as frozen-only, requires it to
read the common VMM's exit RIP, decoded instruction length, and `nextrip`,
requires the portable commit to precede destination-local thaw, and rejects a
regression to the Intel hardware exit-length field.  This is a private-kernel
contract check rather than an Intel architectural oracle.

The non-standard resource-bound inventory also found that the software VMCS
registry hashes GPA page numbers with a mask while its private 64-bucket bound
had no encoded power-of-two invariant.  The header now rejects an invalid
shape at compile time, the collision test constructs its second GPA from the
declared bound instead of a stale literal, and the private ledger records that
this is runtime hash policy rather than an Intel VMCS limit.

## 2026-08-02 — doubled kernel snapshot and private-format review

The forward kernel replay of common vCPU checkpoint state found that the
historical `STRUCT_VM` record is an unversioned host-endian sequence.  It also
saves exception vector and error collateral without saving the
`exception_pending` owner, and omits pending NMI and external-interrupt owners.
Appending provenance or owner bits would break exact record consumption and
would make an old reader interpret a new record incorrectly.  The legacy
record is therefore frozen pending a distinct named `vm-v2` record and an
explicit userspace legacy-selection path.

The first implementation slice is the architecture-neutral `VMS2` outer
envelope in `sys/dev/vmm`, not an amd64 structure dump.  It uses fixed-width
little-endian headers, exact lengths and section counts, typed per-instance
sections, canonical zero reserved fields, and a critical-section flag so a
reader cannot silently ignore state required for correctness.  The builder is
transactional and the reader validates the complete record before exposing a
payload.  Four independent ATF cases cover round trip, failed-builder
non-mutation, truncation and every header boundary, aliases, forged iterator
state, reserved bits, and trailing bytes.

The reverse/private-interface replay then found that a caller could mutate the
public reader cursor after initialization or alias an output object with the
wire image.  Every iterator call now revalidates its local bounds and section
header, and initialization/finalization/iteration reject output aliases.  The
container is recorded as a private versioned compatibility contract, not a
VirtIO or Intel ABI.  It is not yet selected by bhyve: semantic common-vCPU and
architecture-specific sections, unknown-critical dispatch, transactional
kernel restore, named-record selection, legacy decode, and live old/new
checkpoint qualification remain required before integration.

The next semantic slice adds versioned common-VM, common-vCPU, and amd64-vCPU
payload codecs beneath the VMS2 envelope.  Common state carries topology,
startup-wait ownership, and the next program counter.  The amd64 section keeps
x2APIC state, pending-event owners and exact exception provenance, XCR0, and
absolute TSC.  Transient host exit classification, exit RIP, and decoded
instruction length are explicitly excluded.  No native `struct vm_exit`,
`cpuset_t`, pointer, descriptor, lock, C-enum storage, or host padding is part
of the wire image.  Decode checks an unsigned provenance value before enum
conversion, rejects inconsistent exception owner/collateral combinations, and
does not mutate output on failure.  Runtime and wire event enums are separate
private domains joined only by explicit exhaustive adapters.

The doubled kernel review deliberately stops record selection at this point.
NMI and external-interrupt publication is asynchronous, while the legacy
snapshot reads plain owner integers without a shared event fence.  VMS2 must
capture pending exception, NMI, external interrupt, restart cursor, and amd64
collateral under one frozen or generation-checked transaction.  Restore must
copy the complete user record into immutable kernel-owned staging, decode and
validate every vCPU, and only then publish the whole set.  These event-fence
and all-vCPU transaction requirements block `vm-v2` integration; a portable
byte layout alone is not sufficient evidence.

The next independent format replay compiled the shared codecs in an actual
`-nostdinc` kernel translation environment rather than relying on their ATF
inclusion.  It found that the public headers unconditionally included libc
`stdbool.h` and `stdint.h`; kernel builds now select `sys/stdint.h` while the
userland tests retain the standard headers.  The same reverse traversal found
that a caller could forge the public reader cursor to a later valid section.
Each iteration now revalidates the complete immutable envelope and derives the
only legal cursor from `sections_read`, so a valid-section jump cannot reorder
or omit state.  The amd64 semantic review also rejects XCR0 images without the
mandatory x87 bit, a supplied exception error code on a vector that cannot
carry one, and ICEBP/task-switch provenance attached to anything other than
`#DB`.  Missing error collateral remains context-sensitive because the
existing injector suppresses it in real mode.  Native ATF, ASan/UBSan, strict kernel syntax compilation, the 224-row

The restarted reverse kernel-lifetime pass found an operational failure in

That replay also found two non-standard ordering constraints which make a

closed runtime domain, and verifies that the already-restored LAPIC image has

successful, mismatched, invalid, null, aliased, wrapping, and zero-vCPU cases.

The restarted reverse event-lifetime replay found that topology and mode

successful plan could be reused after later events arrived.  Plan creation

and consumes a copied generation-bound MTF owner before performing the final
no-fail publication of all four owners.  Stale publication is tested to leave

### 2026-08-02 — shared-kernel rollback identity and event-driven wait proof

The doubled kernel review continued outside the Intel backend.  Its forward
all-vCPU rollback traversal found a production defect in
`vcpu_set_state_all()`: after a partial transition failure, the rollback loop
iterated the recorded CPU identifiers but repeatedly passed the stale vCPU
pointer from the failed iteration.  The loop now resolves every recorded ID
back to its own live vCPU and performs that member's IDLE transition in all
kernel configurations; an impossible rollback failure remains an invariant
violation.  A source validator pins the identity rule, while installed-kernel
transition fault injection remains a required live gate.

The shared event review then replaced the proposed retry/polling shape with an
architecture-neutral generation wait protocol.  A ticket binds a non-reused
lifecycle owner, the exact wait-state storage, its current generation, and the
exact ticket storage.  The FreeBSD sleepqueue-chain spin lock is the single
interlock for generation publication, predicate recheck, waiter enqueue, and
broadcast.  Therefore a publisher before the lock changes the generation seen
by the waiter; a publisher racing the recheck waits for the chain lock; and a
publisher after the recheck cannot broadcast until the waiter is enqueued.
Cancellation increments the generation when representable, fails closed on
exhaustion, and wakes every waiter.  The mechanism has no timeout, retry
cadence, allocation, sleepable publisher lock, serialized pointer, or guest
ABI.

A consumer-first replay found two malformed-credential cases and now rejects
zero or future ticket generations as stale while preserving caller output.
The final shared-kernel context replay also found that the direct sleepqueue
wrapper lacked the `DROP_GIANT()` / `PICKUP_GIANT()` pairing used by native
FreeBSD interruptible sleep and completion paths.  Although current VMM cdev
operations are MPSAFE, the shared primitive now preserves the kernel-wide
calling contract instead of depending on that unstated caller history.
The wait state now accounts every registered sleeper.  Cancellation wakes
them, the final departing waiter wakes a lifecycle drainer, and
`vmm_event_wait_drain()` waits without a timeout until none remain.  The future
VM adapter must cancel and drain while retaining its enclosing operation/VM
owner before freeing the state.  Reinitializing live state is likewise
forbidden by the lifecycle owner rather than made into a public reset
operation.

Pinned Linux KVM independently uses an interlocked `rcuwait` predicate loop
for shared invalidation state, while pinned QEMU migration code uses events,
conditions, and semaphores rather than fixed-cadence polling.  Those are
behavioral architecture comparisons only.  The sleepqueue implementation is
a reviewed FreeBSD-private kernel detail; the standard-visible requirement is
only lossless event ownership and atomic checkpoint behavior.

The review prompt now ends with two additional independent phases: a fresh
shared-kernel ownership/wakeup replay and a consumer-led non-standard replay
composed with those owners.  Focused value tests cover generation lifecycle,
cancellation and overflow, exact storage identity, aliases, copied tickets,
busy tickets, and transactional rejection.  Production VM lifecycle wiring,
installed-kernel signal/drain/teardown races, live checkpoint
publication, and non-amd64 builds remain explicit gates rather than inferred
successes.

After the final kernel-context correction, the normal rootless model passes
163 cases, the final combined ASan/UBSan model passes the same 163 cases, the
validator accepts 231 requirements and 64 private interfaces with every

## 2026-08-02 final-source kernel and private-boundary replay

The requested doubled review is now stronger than the earlier two-pass gate.
VirtIO/VSOCK adds final-source Passes R and S, and nested VMX adds Passes 19
and 20.  They independently restart from teardown/asynchronous publication and
from retained private-interface consumers after every correction.  The nested
requirements validator requires all four new phase headings.

The kernel replay found four coordinator defects before VM integration: group
finish/abort consumed and zeroed the caller checkpoint before unlock lookup;
checkpoint transaction identities were unique only within one VM; and a
separate enter-then-defer API allowed checkpoint reopen between classification
and deferral.  It also found caller vCPU membership was validated before the
transaction lock and copied only after it had already selected and quiesced
owners.  The coordinator now stages, validates, and uses immutable transaction
membership under its transaction lock,
allocates VM and transaction identities from one global non-reused domain, and
atomically admits or defers idempotent events under the same per-vCPU spin
lock.  Cancellation also closes deferred-event admission.  These fixes are
recorded as NVMX-EVENT-016 and private policy NVMX-PRIVATE-065.  The object
remains deliberately unattached pending installed-kernel multi-VM identity,
signal, cancellation, finish/abort, teardown, and fault qualification.

### 2026-08-02 — doubled VMX-instruction and private-memory-boundary review

The fresh kernel-first pass started from the frozen VMX-instruction consumer
and independently traced every callback length into the private guest-memory
adapter.  It found that VMXON, VMCLEAR, and VMPTRLD decoded only a 64-bit
physical address but asked the callback to read a 16-byte scratch buffer, and
that VMPTRST encoded the architecturally required 64-bit current-VMCS pointer
but asked it to write the same 16-byte length.  The reads could fault beyond a
valid operand; the write could also overwrite the following eight L1 bytes.
All four instructions now access exactly eight bytes.  Focused tests place
VMXON, VMPTRLD, and VMPTRST operands at the final eight bytes of the mapping
and separately record callback addresses and lengths, so copying only the
implementation's value without exercising its memory extent cannot satisfy
the test.

The non-standard replay classifies the mapping-size and scatter/gather limits
as private adapter resource policy, not Intel architecture.  The requirements
validator now pins the architectural VMPTRST width independently beside those
private bounds.  Missing callbacks continue to return a host implementation
error and never become a guest VMfail result.  Live Intel instruction-fault
priority and page-boundary qualification remain in the hardware evidence
ledger rather than being inferred from the rootless callback model.

The reverse test-consumer pass also found that the live VMX-instruction group
named only requirements 001 through 003.  Operand decoding, exact memory
widths, permission priority, frozen publication, internal arbitration, visible
control reconstruction, and retryable commit ownership could therefore remain
outside that group's declared evidence.  The group now names all ten
`NVMX-INST` requirements and requires page-boundary operands with adjacent
canaries for VMXON, VMCLEAR, VMPTRLD, and VMPTRST.  The validator rejects a
future narrowing of either the requirement set or that live boundary test.

### 2026-08-02 — doubled hardware-entry result ownership review

The next kernel-first pass traced every hardware VM-entry outcome from the
processor adapter through classification, VMCS02/MSR unwind, architectural
context publication, event commit or abort, and caller rejection output.  It
found that the private classified-result structure behaved like a loose group
of fields at its destructive consumer: an L2-exit or L0-failure disposition
could also carry a separately valid stale L1 rejection image.  Production
classification happened to zero that member, but the boundary did not prove
the invariant before committing or unwinding hardware ownership.

The result is now validated as a closed sum type.  Only a proven L2 exit may
commit launch ownership; only the rejection disposition may carry exactly one
canonical validated architectural rejection; L2 exit and L0 failure require a
canonical empty rejection.  The finish boundary performs this check before
any VMCS, MSR, context, event, or caller-output mutation.  Negative tests inject
valid-but-contradictory rejection images into both other dispositions and
prove complete owner and output preservation.  This composition rule is
explicitly recorded as private policy `NVMX-PRIVATE-085`; it is not presented
as an Intel wire structure.

The standards-facing replay then found a separate architectural indexing
error in the failed-entry conversion helper.  Intel SDM 29.8 defines an
MSR-load failure qualification as one-based, explicitly assigning value 1 to
the first entry; pinned Linux KVM independently returns `i + 1`.  The helper
had accepted zero and rejected the last entry as though the field were
zero-based, and its old test repeated that assumption.  It now accepts exactly
1 through the advertised entry count, the canonical rejection validator
rejects qualification zero, and independent fixtures cover the first entry,
last entry, zero, and one-past-the-end.

### 2026-08-02 — doubled active-L2 restore and dispatch-boundary review

The next kernel replay followed an active L2 from the portable continuation
through per-vCPU decoding, destination-local MSR scratch and VPID staging, the
VM-wide VMCS-registry swap, and final per-vCPU publication.  The snapshot ioctl
is correctly registered with the all-vCPU lock and therefore enters the
architecture callback with every live vCPU frozen.  The publication transaction
also validates all fallible workspace and registry operations before its final
infallible assignments and rolls earlier workspace acquisitions back on a late

The reverse non-standard review nevertheless found that both architecture
helpers treated the dispatch-table freeze as an unchecked remote assumption.
That coupling was safe for the current caller but fragile under an internal
caller or future ioctl-table refactor: destination scratch could be staged, or
a VM-wide registry could be published, beside a running vCPU.  The outer
architecture snapshot callback now checks the freeze before any
ordinary VMCS or register image can be restored; per-vCPU nested staging checks
again before private scratch allocation; and VM-wide restore completion checks
every live destination immediately before publication.  Each returns `EBUSY`
if the contract is lost.  The private contract is recorded as
`NVMX-PRIVATE-086`, and the validator pins all three local checks plus the
existing all-vCPU dispatch.

### 2026-08-02 — doubled SCSI kernel and private-state review

The device-first pass traced CTL commands, request-worker ownership, event
